sections.title: Overlapping events
sections.content:
When we talk about two events or activities that went on over the same period of past time, we can often use the past continuous or the past simple for both:
• Mia was reading to the children while Ben was washing up. (or ... read ... washed up.)
Using the past continuous emphasises that the event or activity ('was reading') was in progress during the past period of time ('while Ben was washing up'). Compare:
• When I was learning / learned to drive I was living with my parents.
Was learning emphasises that the activity was in progress ('I had lessons during this time') and learned emphasises completion ('I passed my test during this time').
When we talk about two or more past completed events that followed one another, we use the past simple, not the past continuous, for both (see also Unit 5C):
• She got up when the alarm clock went off.

sections.title: Repeated past actions
sections.content:
We usually use the past simple rather than the past continuous to talk about repeated past actions:
• We went to Spain three times last year.
• Did you drive past her house every day?
However, we can use the past continuous, particularly in spoken English, when we want to emphasise that repeated actions went on for a limited and temporary period of past time:
• When Kata was in hospital, we were visiting her twice a day. (or ... we visited ...)
• To lose weight before the race, I wasn't eating any biscuits for weeks. (or ... I didn't eat ...)
or to talk about something that happened surprisingly often:
• Last week I was having to bring work home every night to get it all done. (or ... had ...)
• When the builders were here I was making them cups of tea all the time. (or ... made ...)

sections.title: Narrative structure
sections.content:
We often use the past simple in a narrative (e.g. a report or a story) to talk about a single complete past event and the past continuous to describe the situation that existed at the time. The event might have interrupted the situation, or happened while the situation was in progress:
• Erika dropped her bag while she was getting into her car.
• She was shaking with anger as she left the hotel.

sections.title: Unfulfilled intentions
sections.content:
We can use either the past continuous or past simple (or past perfect; see Unit 5E) with some verbs to talk about things we intended to do but didn't:
• We were meaning to call in and see you, but Marc wasn't feeling well. (or We meant ...)
Also: consider + -ing, expect to, hope to, intend to, plan to / on + -ing, think about / of + -ing, want to
These verbs (with the exception of mean) and wonder about can also be used with the present and past continuous to report what we might do in the future. The past continuous is less definite than the present continuous:
• I was thinking of going to China next year, but it depends how much money I've got. (less definite than I'm thinking of going ...)
• We were wondering about inviting Eva over tomorrow. (less definite than We're wondering about ...)

exercises.question: Just as I ___ into the bath, all the lights ___ off.
exercises.hint: Past continuous for the situation in progress, past simple for the interrupting event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was getting / went
Use the past continuous for the longer background action and the past simple for the shorter interrupting event. Here, the ongoing activity was in progress when a single completed event occurred. The signal is often when + past simple interrupting the past continuous.

exercises.question: She ___ (read) when the phone rang.
exercises.hint: Background activity in progress when interrupted → past continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was reading
The past continuous describes a longer background action in progress when a shorter interrupting event (past simple) occurred. Here, 'reading' is the background; 'rang' is the interruption.

exercises.question: I ___ to go away this weekend, but my boss ___ me some work that I have to finish by Monday. (hope / give)
exercises.hint: Unfulfilled intention vs the single completed event that prevented it.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was hoping / gave
Use the past continuous for the longer background action and the past simple for the shorter interrupting event. Here, the ongoing activity was in progress when a single completed event occurred. The signal is often when + past simple interrupting the past continuous.

exercises.question: It ___ (rain) all morning, so we stayed indoors.
exercises.hint: Continuous background condition during a past period → past continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was raining
The past continuous describes a condition or activity that was ongoing throughout a past period, providing the background context for other events.

exercises.question: When I ___ in Paris, I ___ three hours a day travelling to and from work. (live / spend)
exercises.hint: Background situation vs repeated past action.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was living / spent
The past continuous sets the background scene for a narrative. It describes what was already happening when the main events (past simple) occurred. The past continuous creates the context; the past simple moves the story forward.

exercises.question: While I ___ dinner, my brother arrived home unexpectedly.
exercises.hint: Background activity in progress when interrupted → past continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was cooking
The past continuous ('was cooking') describes the ongoing background activity. The shorter interrupting event ('arrived') uses the past simple. 'While' signals that two events overlapped — use past continuous for the longer one.

exercises.question: A friendly American couple ___ to him as he ___ at the hotel reception.
exercises.hint: Single event interrupting a background situation.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: started / was checking in
Use the past continuous for the longer background action and the past simple for the shorter interrupting event. Here, the ongoing activity was in progress when a single completed event occurred. The signal is often when + past simple interrupting the past continuous.

exercises.question: They ___ all evening, but finally reached an agreement just before midnight.
exercises.hint: Extended activity throughout a past period → past continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: were arguing
The past continuous describes an activity that continued throughout a period ('all evening'). It provides the ongoing background against which other events occur. 'All + time period' is a strong signal for the past continuous.

exercises.question: I bumped into Lena last week. She ___ a lot better than when I last ___ her.
exercises.hint: Temporary past situation vs single event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was looking / saw
Use the past continuous for the longer background action and the past simple for the shorter interrupting event. Here, the ongoing activity was in progress when a single completed event occurred. The signal is often when + past simple interrupting the past continuous.

exercises.question: They were arguing all evening and then suddenly ___ talking.
exercises.hint: Sudden completed event ending a background activity → past simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: stopped
'Suddenly' signals a sharp, completed change — past simple. The ongoing background (were arguing) gives way to the sudden event (stopped). 'Suddenly' almost always signals past simple when describing a narrative event.

exercises.question: My boss ___ into the office just as I ___ everyone my holiday photos.
exercises.hint: Single interrupting event vs action in progress.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: came / was showing
Use the past continuous for the longer background action and the past simple for the shorter interrupting event. Here, the ongoing activity was in progress when a single completed event occurred. The signal is often when + past simple interrupting the past continuous.

exercises.question: They ___ all evening, then suddenly stopped talking.
exercises.hint: Extended ongoing activity throughout a period → past continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: were arguing
The past continuous describes activity ongoing throughout a time period. "All evening" signals the extended duration. The background activity (arguing) is described with past continuous; the sudden end (stopped) uses past simple.

exercises.question: I ___ badminton four times a week before I ___ my ankle.
exercises.hint: Repeated past action (emphasising a limited period) vs single interrupting event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was playing / broke
Use the past continuous for the longer background action and the past simple for the shorter interrupting event. Here, the ongoing activity was in progress when a single completed event occurred. The signal is often when + past simple interrupting the past continuous.

exercises.question: They were arguing all evening, then suddenly ___ talking.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: stopped
"Suddenly" signals a sharp, completed change — past simple. The ongoing background (were arguing) gives way to the sudden completed event (stopped). Narrative sequence: ongoing → sudden interruption.

exercises.question: The smoke alarm ___ when he ___ a candle underneath it. (go off / light)
options: had been going off / had been lighting
exercises.hint: Two completed events, one following the other.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: went off / lit
Two completed events, one following the other.

exercises.question: I can't remember how to answer this question. I must confess that I ___ while the teacher ___ it to us.
exercises.hint: Two activities going on over the same period.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: wasn't listening / was explaining
Two activities going on over the same period. The past continuous describes an action in progress at a specific past moment. It provides the background context, while the past simple describes the completed events that happened against that background.

exercises.question: She ___ more salt to the soup, and then it ___ much better.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: added / tasted
The past simple is used for both actions when they are completed events that happened one after the other in sequence. The order is clear from the context.

exercises.question: Although the television was on, I ___ it. Instead I ___ about my holidays.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: wasn't watching / was dreaming
The past continuous sets the background scene for a narrative. It describes what was already happening when the main events (past simple) occurred. The past continuous creates the context; the past simple moves the story forward.

exercises.question: She ___ open the door and ___ into the room.
options: had been pushing / had been running
exercises.explanation:
Answer: pushed / ran
Use the past simple for a series of completed sequential actions in the past. Each action is finished before the next begins. No perfect tense is needed when the sequence is clear from the narrative.
